segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The strongbox sat dripping on the boards of Maud Brennick's boat, with the harbour flat and bright on every side of it. Walter Ames knelt down in front of it and put his palms on his thighs. Nobody told him to be quick, though the hammer frame was due out of the Shoreside yard that afternoon.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: You don't have to be the one.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She wrote that she'd not ask another to pay it. I'd look poorly beside her if I did.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He laid the oilcloth letter by his knee and set his right hand flat on the smooth plate.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: Ames.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The word went out across the water and the water did nothing at all with it. A gull came over the mast line and kept going. Liora Quill hung at the gunwale with her elbows up on the boards and did not climb in.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: Ames.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory Brennick saw the plate go darker. Not wet-dark. The other way, the way a coal goes when the fire has finished with it.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: Ames.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the cold came up out of it. Jory could see exactly where it had got to. The skin of Walter's hand went white in a line across the knuckles, and the line climbed past the wrist and under the cuff, the way frost climbs a window from the bottom corner. Walter did not take his hand away. Inside the box something heavy turned over once and stopped.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The lid lifted half an inch on its own.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter sat back on his heels and held the hand against his chest. The tips of his fingers were the colour of candle wax. He opened and closed them, and they came back slowly, and not all the way.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Let me see that hand.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: In a moment. It's open.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He raised the lid with his left hand. There were no bottles in it. Nothing stoppered, nothing with a dose already measured out. There was a book bound in leather gone black, with a brown tide-mark running across the lower third of every page. Beside the book lay a lump the size of a fist, wrapped in oiled sailcloth and tied with cord.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: That's not medicine.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: No. That's better. That's how.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory picked up the wrapped lump and worked the cord off with his thumbnail. The sailcloth fell open. The stone inside was grey and dull as a street cobble until he turned it, and then a green came up through it and went out again, like a fish under a hull.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Put it down.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: I've held worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud took it off him anyway and held it in the sailcloth without touching it. Walter was looking at the book, and at his own fingers, and he had begun to cry a little in the way old men do, without changing his face.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Mr Ames. For my book, so it's set down proper. Whose cellar was that, and whose box?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter opened his mouth. His breath came out. He tried it again, and the sound that should have been his name was not in him, the way a step is not there in the dark. He touched his own throat.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: Walter. I can say Walter. I can say my grandmother. I cannot say the other.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Try it slow.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: I have. Twice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He put his good hand on the open lid and looked at the smooth dark plate.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: That was the price. She paid it to shut the thing and I've paid it to open it. She might have told me it was the name itself, but I don't suppose she knew.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nobody answered. Maud was still holding the wrapped stone, turning it an inch at a time in the sailcloth, and her face had changed.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Jory. I've had three of these through my hands since the spring. Off the bottom, out past the dyers' yard, where the floor of the harbour cracked open. Boys bring them in and nobody will buy them.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Same stone?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Same stone. Which means she wrote her measures against the very stuff we're still pulling up. Twenty years dead, and she's the only hand that ever wrote them down.
